container-title: Attacks, Defenses and Testing for Deep Learning

items.abstract: <jats:p>Adversarial detectors based on deep learning have demonstrated high accuracy in identifying perturbed inputs when the attack method is known and the victim model is accessible during detector training. However, in real-world deployment scenarios, attackers rarely operate under these white-box assumptions. This study investigates a critical but underexplored failure mode: the significant performance degradation of AI-based detectors when transferred from whitebox attack settings to black-box transfer attack settings. We systematically train multiple deep learning detectors on adversarial examples generated by a suite of white-box gradient-based methods (FGSM, PGD, and CW) targeting a known victim classifier. We then evaluate these detectors against black-box transfer attacks, where the adversarial examples are generated against a different surrogate model and subsequently transferred to an unknown target model. Our empirical results reveal a consistent and substantial generalization gap, with detection accuracy dropping by an average of 32-47% across all tested architectures. Through ablation studies and feature-space analysis, we identify three primary causes of this failure: (i) overfitting to the specific gradient directions and loss landscapes of the training victim model, (ii) the detector's reliance on attack-specific noise patterns that do not survive model-to-model transfer, and (iii) a fundamental distribution shift between white-box and black-box adversarial manifolds. We further demonstrate that simply increasing detector capacity or training on multiple attack types does not bridge this gap, suggesting that current detection paradigms are inherently brittle to the surrogate-target model mismatch. Our findings establish a new benchmark for evaluating detector robustness under realistic threat models and highlight the urgent need for attack-agnostic detection frameworks that generalize beyond the training environment.</jats:p>
title: The Generalization Gap: Why AI Detectors Trained on White-Box Attacks Fail Against Black-Box Transfer Attacks

items.abstract: <jats:p>Once the box is opened, B2A2 's will baffle most existing control frameworks within modern corporate environments, and potentially spark another pandemic. They must be designed with a minimum set of requirements on transparency and controls. The discussion herein mostly focuses on investment banks, but the principles or frameworks are universal.</jats:p>
title: Black-Box AI Agents (B2A2 ) inside Pandora's Box
